items.title: Paths, active paths, and d-separation in a finite DAG
items.statement:
A **finite directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a finite vertex set $V$ with an
arrow set $E\subseteq V\times V$ and no directed cycle. A **path** from $u$ to
$v$ is a finite sequence of distinct vertices beginning at $u$ and ending at
$v$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction;
the arrows are not required to point along the sequence. An internal vertex of
a path is a **collider on that path** when the two arrows on the path both point
into it, and is a **noncollider** otherwise. A vertex $w$ is a **descendant** of
$v$ if there is a directed path from $v$ to $w$; for this definition
$\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ includes $v$ itself as well as its descendants.

For pairwise disjoint vertex sets $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, a path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is **active given $C$** when every internal noncollider is outside $C$ and
every internal collider has at least one member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in
$C$. The set $C$ **d-separates** $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ when no path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is active given $C$; write $X\perp_d Y\mid C$ in $G$. The empty set of
vertices is allowed for any of $X,Y,C$; in particular d-separation is vacuous
if either endpoint set is empty.

For $T\subseteq V$, $G_{\underline T}$ is obtained by deleting every arrow
whose tail lies in $T$, and $G_{\overline T}$ by deleting every arrow whose
head lies in $T$. These are graph operations only; they do not by themselves
specify a probability law under intervention.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-1, pp. 671–672
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Fine Point 6.1, pp. 78–79

items.title: Finite products of probability kernels are probability kernels
items.statement:
Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Measure Theory, Theorem 5.14
Terence Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory, Proposition 1.7.11

items.axiom_use: The products are finite and the factors are probability measures; no choice axiom is used.

items.title: Recursive structural causal models on finite DAGs
items.statement:
Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values
$X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$; the interventional law is their joint law. The
response map $(a,\omega)\mapsto X_w^a(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, by
induction through the finite topological order and joint measurability of each
$f_v$. This permits evaluation at a random treatment value, such as
$X_w^{M^a}$. When $I=\{A\}$, write $X_w^a$ for the response under
$do(A=a)$. If the factual treatment is $A$, then on $\{A=a\}$ recursion
gives $X_w=X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-2, pp. 672–674
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Technical Points 6.1–6.3, pp. 72–74

items.title: The ancestral moral graph of a DAG
items.statement:
For $S\subseteq V$, its **ancestral set** is
$$\operatorname{An}_G(S):=\{v\in V:\text{there is a directed path from }v\text{ to some }s\in S\},$$
where paths of length zero are allowed, so $S\subseteq\operatorname{An}_G(S)$.
The induced directed subgraph on this set keeps exactly the arrows of $G$
whose two endpoints lie in $\operatorname{An}_G(S)$. Its **moral graph** is
the undirected simple graph obtained by replacing every arrow by an
undirected edge and joining every distinct pair of parents of a common child
by an undirected edge; loops and duplicate edges are discarded. This
undirected graph is the **ancestral moral graph** on $S$ and is denoted
$\operatorname{mor}_G(S)$.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-1, p. 672
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Fine Point 6.1, pp. 78–79

items.title: Faithfulness of a law to a DAG
items.statement:
Assume AC, and let a joint law $P$ on the measurable vertex variables of a
finite DAG $G$ be given. The law is **faithful to $G$** if, for every triple
of pairwise disjoint vertex sets $A,B,C$, the conditional independence
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C)$$
implies that $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$. This is the converse of the
global Markov implication; faithfulness is a separate assumption on the
specified law, not a consequence of DAG factorization. No claim about Markov
equivalence, skeletons, or unshielded colliders is included. Here $X_A$ is
the finite random vector $(X_v)_{v\in A}$ with the finite-product
sigma-algebra; for $A=\varnothing$ it is the unique random element of the
empty-product singleton.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-1, pp. 671–672
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Fine Point 6.2, pp. 79–80

items.axiom_use: Assume AC as required by the conditional-independence definition.

items.title: A Markovian recursive SCM has a topological kernel factorization
items.statement:
Let a finite Markovian recursive SCM be as in
[[def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag]], with topological order
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$. For each $v$, let $\nu_v$ be the law of $U_v$ and define
$$K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},B) :=\nu_v\{u:f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},u)\in B\},\qquad B\in\mathcal S_v.$$
Then $K_v$ is a probability kernel from the parent-coordinate product to
$(S_v,\mathcal S_v)$. If $n=0$, the full-joint law (and the only possible
interventional law) is the point mass on the empty-product singleton. For
$n\ge1$, the full-joint law is the iterated topological composition
$$\mu(dx_{v_1},\ldots,dx_{v_n}) :=K_{v_1}(dx_{v_1})\prod_{r=2}^n K_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},dx_{v_r}).$$
For $n\ge1$ and an intervention $do(X_I=a)$, the same formula holds with the factor
$K_v$ replaced by the point mass $\delta_{a_v}$ for each $v\in I$; all other
factors are unchanged. Marginalizing latent coordinates means taking the
pushforward to $\prod_{v\in O}S_v$ and does not in general produce a
factorization on the observed-only induced graph.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-2, pp. 672–674
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Technical Points 6.1–6.3, pp. 72–74

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used. The exogenous family is finite; its product law, the structural kernels and their finite composition are supplied by the stated choice-free suppliers.

items.title: Every active finite route contains an active path

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-1, pp. 671–672

items.axiom_use: Only finite graph arguments and a minimum in the natural numbers are used; no choice axiom is used.
items.statement: In a finite DAG, a **route** is a finite sequence of vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent by an arrow in either direction; repeated vertices are allowed. Collider and noncollider status is assigned to each internal occurrence using its two incident route arrows. A route is **active given $C$** if each noncollider occurrence is outside $C$ and each collider occurrence is an ancestor of $C$, including membership in $C$. If an active route joins vertices $x,y\notin C$ with $x\ne y$, then an active distinct-vertex path joins $x$ and $y$ given $C$.

items.title: D-separation is separation in the ancestral moral graph
items.statement:
For disjoint $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, $C$ d-separates $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ if and
only if deleting $C$ from $\operatorname{mor}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$ leaves no
undirected path from $X$ to $Y$.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-1, p. 672
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Fine Point 6.1, pp. 78–79

items.axiom_use: The graph is finite, so the finite path and shortening arguments use no choice axiom.

items.title: Conditional independence under kernel extension and conditioning

references.title: Aldous–Chewi, Probability Theory, Lecture 9, Definition 9.1 and Lemma 9.2, printed pp. 35–36

items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the conditional-expectation and conditional-independence interfaces. No regular conditional distribution is constructed.
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $L,R,C,V$ be random elements in arbitrary measurable spaces. Suppose $L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C)$ and that the joint law of $(L,R,C,V)$ is obtained from the law of $(L,R,C)$ by a probability kernel $K(l,c,dv)$ depending only on $(l,c)$. Then
$$ (L,V)\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C),\qquad L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C,V). $$
No regular conditional law on an unspecified measurable space is assumed: $K$ is supplied in the hypotheses.

items.title: DAG factorization implies the global Markov property
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be random elements in measurable spaces
whose joint law is generated, in a topological order of the finite DAG $G$,
by probability kernels $K_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},dx_v)$. For pairwise
disjoint $A,B,C\subseteq V$, if $C$ d-separates $A$ and $B$ in $G$, then
$$\sigma(X_A)\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(X_B)\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
This is the global Markov implication. Its converse is the separate
faithfulness condition in [[def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model]].

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-1, pp. 671–672
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Fine Point 6.1, pp. 78–79

items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the conditional-expectation and conditional-independence interfaces. The finite graph elimination and kernel construction use no further choice.

items.title: The backdoor criterion implies conditional exchangeability
items.statement:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian recursive SCM on $G$. Let $T,W$ be disjoint
vertex sets and let $C$ be a set of nondescendants of $T$. Define the
response-family sigma-algebra
$$\mathcal R_W^T:=\sigma\{X_w^t:w\in W,\ t\in\prod_{v\in T}S_v\}.$$
If $C$ d-separates $T$ and $W$ in $G_{\underline T}$, then
$$\sigma(X_T)\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal R_W^T\mid\sigma(X_C).$$
For each fixed intervention value $t$, this implies
$X_W^t\perp\!\!\!\perp X_T\mid\sigma(X_C)$. No treatment-positivity
condition is needed.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §3-1, pp. 674–675
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, §7.2 and Technical Point 7.1, pp. 87–88

items.axiom_use: Assume AC as required by the conditional-expectation and conditional-independence interfaces. The finite response-copy construction uses no further choice.

items.title: Backdoor adjustment identifies an interventional law
items.statement:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian SCM on a finite DAG $G$. Let $A$ be an
observed countable-valued treatment, $Y$ an observed standard-Borel outcome,
and $L$ an observed finite vector of standard-Borel vertices containing no
descendant of $A$. Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$. Suppose (i) $L$
d-separates $A$ and $Y$ in $G_{\underline A}$ and (ii) a regular conditional
propensity $e_a(L)=P(A=a\mid L)$ is strictly positive $P_L$-almost surely.
Then for every Borel set $B$ in the state space of $Y$,
$$P(Y^a\in B)=\int P(Y\in B\mid A=a,L=l)\,P_L(dl).$$
The right side depends only on the observed law. Thus the law of $Y^a$ is an
identifiable estimand on any statistical model consisting of such SCMs with
the same observed variables. If $Y$ is real and $Y^a$ is integrable, applying
the identity to bounded truncations and taking limits gives
$$E[Y^a]=\int E(Y\mid A=a,L=l)\,P_L(dl).$$
For a continuous treatment, the corresponding regular conditional formula is
identified only for $P_A$-almost every $a$; this theorem makes no pointwise
claim at a null treatment value.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §3-1, pp. 674–675
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, §§7.2–7.3, pp. 87–89

items.axiom_use: Assume AC for regular conditional distributions, disintegration and conditional independence. No further choice is used.

items.title: Counterfactual identities under the front-door conditions
items.statement:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian recursive SCM on a full DAG with observed
vertices $A,M,Y$ and any number of latent vertices. Suppose: (i) every
directed path from $A$ to $Y$ contains $M$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are
d-separated by the empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$
d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in $G_{\underline M}$. For each supplied value
$a\in S_A$, let $M^a$ be the response under $do(A=a)$. Define
$$I_M=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline A}}(M)\setminus\{A\},\qquad I_Y=\operatorname{An}_{G_{\overline M}}(Y)\setminus\{M\},$$
where ancestry includes the vertex itself and $U_I$ is the finite vector of
exogenous coordinates $(U_v)_{v\in I}$. Then $M^a$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_M})$, each response $Y^m$ is measurable with
respect to $\sigma(U_{I_Y})$, and
$$M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp A,\qquad I_M\cap I_Y=\varnothing,\qquad M^a\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y},\qquad M\perp\!\!\!\perp U_{I_Y}\mid A.$$
The recursive responses also satisfy $Y^a=Y^{M^a}$ almost surely. The
conditional independence is for the factual law; it supplies a genuine
conditional product law for the exogenous coordinates used by the outcome
response.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §3-2, pp. 675–676
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Technical Point 7.4, p. 101

items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the conditional-independence statement. The exogenous-coordinate separation uses finite sets and no further choice.

items.title: Front-door adjustment identifies an interventional mean
items.statement:
Assume AC and a finite Markovian SCM with observed countable-valued
treatment $A$, observed standard-Borel mediator $M$, and real outcome $Y$.
Fix an atom $a$ with $P(A=a)>0$. Suppose in the full DAG: (i) $M$ lies on
every directed path from $A$ to $Y$; (ii) $A$ and $M$ are d-separated by the
empty set in $G_{\underline A}$; and (iii) $A$ d-separates $M$ and $Y$ in
$G_{\underline M}$. Write $\mu_a=P(M\in\cdot\mid A=a)$ and, for every
positive-probability treatment atom $a'$, write
$\mu_{a'}=P(M\in\cdot\mid A=a')$. Assume the nested-law support condition
$$\mu_a\ll\mu_{a'}\qquad\text{for every }a'\text{ with }P(A=a')>0,$$
and absolute integrability of the nested conditional means:
$$\int\!\int E(|Y|\mid M=m,A=a')\,P_A(da')\,\mu_a(dm)<\infty.$$
Then
$$E[Y^a]=\int P(dm\mid A=a)\int E(Y\mid M=m,A=a')\,P_A(da').$$
The right side is determined by the observed law, so the interventional mean
is identifiable on any statistical model of SCMs satisfying these
assumptions. For a discrete mediator, the support condition says that every
mediator value having positive probability under $A=a$ also has positive
probability under every positive-probability treatment atom. These are
sufficient conditions only. For non-atomic treatment values, regular
conditional formulas are determined only $P_A$-almost everywhere; this
item makes no pointwise claim at a null treatment value.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §3-2, pp. 675–676
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Technical Point 7.4, p. 101

items.axiom_use: Assume AC for the regular conditional laws, disintegration and conditional-expectation interfaces. The finite structural recursion and countable treatment mixture use no further choice.

items.title: A confounder and a conditioned collider
items.statement:
Consider first a confounding SCM with independent $U\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$
and $E\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/4)$, observed $A=U\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}E$,
and observed $Y=U$. Its DAG is $U\to A$ and $U\to Y$. The only path between
$A$ and $Y$ is the backdoor path $A\leftarrow U\to Y$.

For collider conditioning, let independent $B,C\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$,
and set $D=B\lor C$. Its DAG is $B\to D\leftarrow C$.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §2-1 and §3-1, pp. 671–675
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Fine Point 6.1 and §7.1, pp. 78, 85–86

items.title: The same observed law can have different intervention laws
items.statement:
Let $U\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$. In SCM 1 set $A=U$ and $Y=A$; its graph
is $U\to A\to Y$. In SCM 2 set $A=U$ and $Y=U$; its graph is
$U\to A$ and $U\to Y$. Degenerate independent exogenous errors at $A$ and
$Y$ complete both Markovian SCMs.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §3-1, pp. 674–675
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, §6.1, pp. 71–74

items.title: A binary SCM where front-door adjustment works
items.statement:
Let $U\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$,
$E_A\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/4)$, and
$E_M\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/5)$ be mutually independent. Set
$$A=U\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}E_A,\qquad M=A\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}E_M,\qquad Y=M\lor U.$$
The full graph is $U\to A$, $U\to Y$, $A\to M$, $M\to Y$. The only directed
$A$-to-$Y$ path passes through $M$; there is no backdoor path from $A$ to
$M$; and the backdoor path $M\leftarrow A\leftarrow U\to Y$ is blocked by
$A$. Both mediator values have positive probability conditional on either
treatment value, so the nested conditional laws have the required support.

references.title: Judea Pearl, Causal Diagrams for Empirical Research, §3-2, pp. 675–676
Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If, Technical Point 7.4, p. 101
